title: Rose and the Stolen Supper Spell
paragraphs: It was pasta pesto night in Amsterdam, and pasta pesto night was the best night of the week.
Rose sat at the kitchen table with Foxy on her lap.
Foxy was her cuddly fox, soft and orange, and he came everywhere.
Outside, the lady next door shouted, "My pesto's gone!"
"Mine too!" called the man on the houseboat.
Rose looked out of the window.
A line of footprints ran along the street.
Small, pointy, and bright, bright green.
Rose tucked Foxy under her arm.
They followed the green footprints along the canal and into the Enchanted Forest, where the leaves whispered as Rose went by.
Deep in the forest, the footprints led to a little stream.
Rose bent down and touched one of the green footprints.
Some of the green came off on her finger.
Rose dipped her finger in the stream.
The green fizzed and went pop, like a bubble.
She whispered to Foxy, "Let's remember that."
Across the stream, in a clearing, stood a cauldron bigger than a bath.
It was full to the top with pesto.
Stirring it with a long wooden spoon was a witch.
She had a patched red hat, wild white hair, and long green fingers that glowed.
The witch peered down at her.
I wiggled my magic green fingers, and every drop came to me.
And tonight I'm eating the lot.
"It is if I say it is," said the witch.
Rose looked at those glowing green fingers.
Green, just like the magic on the footprints.
Daddy stepped forward in his most polite grown-up voice.
That pesto belongs to Amsterdam, and I must ask..."
"Boring!" said the witch, and she wiggled one finger at him.
Rose clapped a hand over her mouth.
Daddy could only say one word.
"And because you interrupted, I'm not waiting.
I'm eating it all right now."
Rose held Foxy up to her ear.
Foxy was very good at ideas.
"Foxy says," said Rose, nice and loud, "that you can't eat with hands like those."
Everybody knows you wash your hands before you eat."
"I haven't washed my hands for three hundred years."
"Then your pesto will taste of three hundred years of dirty hands.
"But if you wash them," said Rose, "Daddy says food tastes ten times better."
The witch looked at her fingers.
The witch put her hands in the stream.
They went pop, pop, pop, like bubbles.
The last of the green fizzed away.
And with the magic washed off, all her spells came undone.
Behind them, the cauldron gave an enormous gurgle.
All at once, it was empty.
Every drop of pesto had gone back home, to the jars of Amsterdam.
The witch sat down on the grass with a bump.
"I only wanted something nice for pudding."
Then she said, "You can come to our house on pasta night.
"But you have to wash your hands first."
The witch held up her clean pink fingers, and she smiled a wobbly, crooked, very nearly kind smile.
Rose and Daddy walked home as the sun went down.
In every kitchen in Amsterdam, the pesto jars were full again.
Daddy stirred some into the pasta, and Rose ate every last bit, with Foxy beside her bowl.
And for pudding, they had strawberries.

title: The Tiger in the Racing Seat
paragraphs: Santosh's racing car had two seats, four shiny wheels, and one very serious problem.
"Tiger," Santosh said, "you have to watch the road."
His cuddly orange tiger leaned against the door.
One soft paw rested on the window.
Santosh fastened the little seat belt across Tiger's tummy.
Now the toy sat straight, with his black stripes showing and his stitched smile facing the track.
Dad checked Santosh's helmet and tightened his own glove around the little car's safety strap.
"Stay on the track, and stop if you need help."
Beyond the starting line, the racecourse curled around the park.
There was a wooden bridge, a bend beside the flower beds, and a finish line hung with colorful flags.
A girl in a green car pulled up beside him.
The car rolled forward, then faster.
Over the wooden bridge they went.
Around the flower beds they swept.
The flags flashed red and yellow ahead.
Maya's green car was just in front.
"We can catch her," Santosh told Tiger.
On the bridge, something bounced against Santosh's elbow.
The car drifted toward the edge of the track.
He looked up quickly and straightened the wheel.
At the flower-bed bend, a yellow cone lay across the narrowest part of the track.
Their cars stopped with a small space between them.
"We could drive on the grass," Maya said.
Santosh looked at the soft ground.
Yesterday's rain had left a dark muddy patch beside the bend.
At the edge of the course, Dad spotted him and waved to the race helper.
The helper lifted the fallen cone and set it upright.
This time Santosh watched the bend all the way through.
He turned smoothly, keeping his hands steady.
Maya was still ahead, but not by much.
Santosh felt every bump through his seat.
Tiger bounced once, safely strapped in, and settled against the cushion.
At the final bend, Santosh started turning a little earlier.
The car followed the curve without wobbling.
Santosh pressed the pedal and kept his eyes straight ahead.
He let the car slow to a stop.
For a moment he stared at the flags.
Tiger was still smiling his stitched smile, with both paws pointed forward.
Dad came over and lifted Santosh's helmet.
Santosh thought about the bridge, the fallen cone, and that last smooth turn.
On the walk home, he carried Tiger under one arm.
A small blue ribbon was tied around the toy's paw.
Tiger, who had done absolutely none of the steering, seemed very pleased.

title: Martin, Sofia and the Very Bad Hiders
paragraphs: Martin was very good at hide and seek.
When Sofia hid, she stood in the middle of the room, covered her eyes, and said, "Gone!"
Martin always pretended he couldn't find her.
That was what big brothers did.
One morning, Sofia found a leaf at the bottom of the garden.
It was not an ordinary leaf.
It was as big as an umbrella.
Right at the bottom was a gap, just big enough for two.
And through the gap came a warm wind that smelled of rain and flowers.
It was dark and leafy, and it went on for much longer than a hedge should.
Then, at the very end, there was light.
The grass was taller than Martin.
The ferns were taller than Daddy.
And far away, by a sparkling lake, a whole family of giants with long, long necks was having a drink.
"Dinos!" said Sofia, and she jumped up and down.
Martin was so busy looking that he walked straight into a tree.
It wasn't a tree at all.
And a very long way up was a dinosaur, smiling down at them.
Next to her stood a Tyrannosaurus rex with very tiny arms.
But Rex only had two fingers on each tiny hand.
It was a very skinny tree.
Her head stuck out of the top.
Her tail stuck out of the side.
So Bramble lay down behind the hill.
But her long neck stuck straight up into the sky, like a lamppost.
"When we got here, I thought your leg was a tree.
What if you were the tree?"
"Stand very, very still," said Martin, "and hold your head up high, like the top of a tree."
Bramble lowered her head, and Sofia put one leaf on her nose, very carefully.
Rex counted again, with Sofia's help.
He even looked under a leaf, which was silly, but he was running out of ideas.
At last he leaned against the biggest tree in the forest for a rest.
Rex jumped so high his tiny arms waved.
She walked into the middle of the clearing.
But Martin looked up at Bramble and Rex, and gave them a little wink.
They looked for a very long time.
And in the middle of the clearing, behind her own two hands, Sofia giggled and giggled.
Because that is what big brothers do.
And it turns out, it's what big dinosaurs do too.
